strengths: The paper addresses a useful computer-vision problem: generating complete, individually manipulable tabletop objects with coherent layouts. The integration of instance completion, reconstruction, alignment, and simulation export has practical value.

The reported improvements are substantial across complementary evaluations. On 78 scenes, TabletopGen improves DINOv2 similarity from MIDI’s 0.7070 to 0.8383 and reduces scene-level collisions from 98.72% to 7.69%. The qualitative comparisons also show visibly better object completeness and arrangement.
The randomized human evaluation provides meaningful corroboration beyond automated judging: 126 valid participants prefer the method in 83.13% of comparisons.
The component ablations support the usefulness of the alignment stages, particularly TSA: replacing TSA with direct MLLM estimation raises scene-level collisions from 7.69% to 61.54%.

The presentation is generally clear, with explicit rotation losses, optimization settings, intermediate outputs, prompt templates, and a runtime breakdown. Modular editing and the described manipulation demonstrations illustrate useful applications.
weaknesses: The central claim of accurate pose and metric-scale recovery is insufficiently validated. TSA uses a generated top view and commonsense dimensions, which provide plausible hypotheses rather than measured geometry. No ground-truth rotation, translation, scale, or support-relation errors are reported. Best-of-160-view perceptual similarity cannot establish these geometric claims.

The algorithmic contribution is not adequately isolated. DRO combines established silhouette, contour, and feature losses, while TSA depends heavily on generative-model capabilities. Table 3 compares against direct MLLM parameter prediction, but does not test alternative geometric alignment methods, individual loss terms, simpler anchor choices, or RMA-Score itself. Comparisons using shared instance assets would help distinguish alignment improvements from stronger completion and 3D-generation backbones.

The physical guarantees are overstated. Stacking-order inference and convex-decomposition collision shapes do not guarantee collision-free or stable placement, and Table 1 itself reports collisions in 7.69% of scenes. Collision detection tolerances, treatment of intended contacts, and whether evaluation occurs before or after simulation settling are unspecified. Two described manipulation demonstrations support feasibility but do not establish broad simulation reliability.

The evaluation set is insufficiently documented: the manuscript does not clearly specify image provenance, the real/synthetic split, selection procedures, or difficulty distributions. Quantitative real-image results and breakdowns by occlusion, object density, and stacking complexity are missing, limiting the claimed generalization. Uncertainty estimates are also absent.

Important implementation ambiguities remain despite the useful supplementary material. Section 3.3 describes globally scaling bounding boxes into world coordinates, whereas Section 6.1 says commonsense dimensions are retained unless they deviate significantly, typically rescaling only the table; the threshold and exact rule are not given. Exact ChatGPT/Seedream versions and numerical support-height computation are also unclear. The top-view prompt explicitly requests a rectangular tabletop despite claims covering round and triangular tables.

The demonstrated operating assumptions are narrower than the broad claims: canonical alignment uses right-angle corrections followed by yaw optimization, and the prompts assume object axes parallel to the support plane. Arbitrarily tilted objects, difficult occlusions, and generation failures are not systematically examined. Overall, the promising results make this a close decision, but the missing geometric validation and contribution-specific comparisons favor borderline rejection under Algorithms/General.

strengths: TabletopGen addresses a relevant computer vision problem: generating complete, independently manipulable tabletop objects with coherent layouts. The integration of instance completion, mesh generation, rotation optimization, and spatial alignment is practically motivated and clearly organized.

The reported results demonstrate substantial system-level improvements on the 78-scene test set. Compared with MIDI, DINOv2 similarity increases from 0.7070 to 0.8383, while the percentage of scenes containing collisions decreases from 98.72% to 7.69%. Figure 3 also shows visibly improved object completeness and appearance.

The human evaluation provides meaningful evidence beyond automated model judgments. The supplementary material documents randomized presentation, 126 valid participants after filtering, and an overall preference of 83.13% for TabletopGen.

The component ablations support the usefulness of the proposed alignment pipeline, especially TSA: replacing it with direct MLLM estimation raises scene collision rates from 7.69% to 61.54%. The supplementary prompts, intermediate outputs, optimization settings, and runtime breakdown improve transparency.
weaknesses: The central claims of accurate pose and metric-scale recovery are not directly evaluated. TSA uses a generated top view and commonsense object dimensions, both of which can introduce geometrically plausible but incorrect reconstructions. No ground-truth rotation, translation, dimension, or support-relation measurements establish accuracy. The independently selected best views for LPIPS, DINOv2, and CLIP in Section 8.1 measure appearance similarity but cannot validate recovered 3D structure or absolute scale.

The repeated claims of guaranteed collision-free, physically grounded scenes exceed the method and evidence. Table 1 reports collisions in 7.69% of generated scenes, and neither stacking-order prediction nor adding collision shapes guarantees valid initial placement or stable support. The collision evaluation omits consequential details such as collision geometry, penetration tolerance, treatment of intended support contacts, and whether measurements precede or follow simulation. Section 7 describes two successful manipulation demonstrations, but provides no systematic stability or task-success evaluation.

The experiments establish pipeline-level gains more convincingly than the originality and specific benefit of the proposed alignment mechanisms. DRO combines established silhouette, contour, and perceptual losses; TSA combines generated-view bounding boxes with size priors and an anchor heuristic. Table 3 compares these components only against direct MLLM parameter prediction. Comparisons with geometric alignment alternatives, simpler anchor choices, and individual DRO loss ablations would better establish the contribution. The visual advantage also remains partly confounded by differences in underlying asset-generation models across systems.

The test-set construction is insufficiently documented for the broad robustness claims. Section 4.2 describes scene categories but does not specify image provenance, the proportion of generated versus real inputs, selection criteria, or handling of failed generations. Real-world reconstruction is demonstrated qualitatively rather than through a separately reported quantitative evaluation. Results are not broken down by crowding, occlusion, or stacking complexity, despite these being central motivations.

Several implementation ambiguities hinder reproducibility of the core method. Section 3.3 describes converting all bounding boxes into instance scales through a global factor, whereas Section 6.1 describes retaining commonsense dimensions and rescaling only objects with substantial discrepancies, typically the table; the discrepancy threshold and exact conversion are unspecified. The top-view prompt in Figure 24 explicitly requests a rectangular tabletop despite the claimed support for round and triangular tables. Exact ChatGPT model versions, stochastic retry policies, and important physical parameters are also missing. These concerns, together with the gaps in geometric and physical validation, narrowly outweigh the promising empirical results under the default Algorithms/General assessment.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant computer vision problem: generating complete, individually manipulable tabletop objects with coherent layouts. The unified text/image pipeline and explicit instance representation offer practical value for simulation and scene editing.

The reported comparative results are strong. On 78 scenes, TabletopGen improves DINOv2 similarity from MIDI’s 0.7070 to 0.8383 and reduces scene-level collisions from 98.72% to 7.69%. Figure 3 also shows convincing improvements in object completeness, appearance, and arrangement.

The human evaluation provides useful evidence beyond automated similarity and GPT scores. With 126 valid participants, randomized presentation, and eight scenes per participant, TabletopGen receives 83.13% overall preference and substantially higher ratings across all three criteria.

The component ablations support the usefulness of the alignment pipeline: removing TSA increases scene-level collisions from 7.69% to 61.54%, while removing DRO increases them to 16.67%. The supplement provides prompts, optimization settings, intermediate outputs, and a runtime breakdown, improving transparency.
weaknesses: The central claim of accurate pose and metric-scale recovery is insufficiently validated. A generated top view and commonsense size estimates provide plausible hypotheses, but do not establish recovery of the original geometry. There are no ground-truth rotation, translation, or scale measurements, nor a quantitative assessment of whether top-view generation preserves object identities and positions. Independently selecting the best of 160 views for each perceptual metric further limits what these scores establish about geometric accuracy.

The physical-validity claims exceed the evidence. The manuscript repeatedly describes collision-free or guaranteed physically grounded scenes, although 7.69% of its scenes contain collisions. Stacking-order prediction and convex collision proxies do not themselves guarantee valid support or stable contacts. The collision test, penetration tolerance, treatment of intended contacts, and timing relative to physics simulation are unspecified. The two manipulation demonstrations described in the supplement are encouraging, but do not establish reliability across the evaluation set.

The experimental design does not sufficiently isolate the proposed algorithmic contribution from the strong pretrained components. DRO combines established rendering losses, while TSA relies heavily on generative viewpoint conversion and an anchor heuristic. Replacing entire stages with direct MLLM predictions demonstrates pipeline utility, but does not establish the benefits of the individual losses, RMA anchor selection, or differentiable refinement over coarse search. A comparison using shared generated assets would help separate alignment improvements from asset-quality improvements.

The evaluation set is insufficiently documented: the provenance of the 78 inputs, real-versus-generated composition, selection procedure, and distributions of clutter and occlusion are unclear. Real-image generalization is supported mainly by qualitative examples. Results also lack uncertainty estimates or repeated-generation analysis, leaving robustness to stochastic upstream models unresolved.

Important implementation details remain ambiguous despite the useful supplement. Section 3.3 describes globally converting all bounding boxes to scales, whereas the supplement describes selectively rescaling objects whose commonsense dimensions disagree, typically only the table; the threshold and precise rule are absent. Exact ChatGPT and Seedream versions and the conversion from stacking relations to support heights are also unspecified. With no declared contribution type, I assess this as Algorithms/General: the promising system results bring it close to acceptance, but the unresolved geometric validation and attribution concerns favor borderline rejection.

strengths: TabletopGen addresses an important computer-vision problem: converting a single image or text prompt into separate, physically usable tabletop assets for robotic manipulation. The combination of instance generation, rotation alignment, top-view layout inference, and simulation is coherent and practically relevant.

The comparative results provide substantial evidence of improved scene usability. Across 78 scenes, collision-containing scenes decrease from 98.72% for MIDI to 7.69%, while DINOv2 similarity increases from 0.7070 to 0.8383. Supplementary comparisons include SceneGen and FlashSculptor and strengthen the physical evaluation with support and settling tests; TabletopGen achieves 92.13% dynamic settling stability.

Human evaluation corroborates the automated metrics: 126 valid respondents prefer TabletopGen in 83.13% of comparisons. The qualitative examples also show visibly more complete objects and coherent tabletop arrangements. Ablations demonstrate that both alignment stages contribute, particularly TSA.

The downstream validation goes beyond attractive renderings. Policies fine-tuned on 2,000 synthetic trajectories per task achieve 84%, 80%, and 68% real-world success over 50 trials each on three manipulation tasks. Together with the scene-quality results, this supports a slight preference for acceptance despite the limitations below.
weaknesses: The claimed precise metric reconstruction and collision-free layout recovery exceed what the method establishes. TSA uses a generated top view and commonsense object dimensions, neither of which guarantees faithful geometry or absolute scale. Top-view boxes and stacking relations do not enforce nonpenetration or valid support on arbitrary meshes. There is no ground-truth pose/scale evaluation, and the supplementary description of selectively rescaling inconsistent objects leaves the actual scale-estimation procedure insufficiently specified.

The experiments only partially isolate the proposed algorithmic contribution. DRO combines established silhouette, contour, and perceptual losses, while TSA relies heavily on foundation-model outputs. Replacing either stage with direct ChatGPT parameter prediction is a relatively weak control. Comparisons using identical generated assets with alternative geometric alignment, plus ablations of RMA anchor selection and DRO refinement versus its existing coarse search, would better establish the source of improvement.

Generalization evidence is limited relative to the broad claims. The 78-scene benchmark contains 74 synthetic images and only four real photographs. Best-view image similarity measures perceptual agreement rather than 3D layout accuracy; averaging similarity to the same input photograph over other views does not establish multiview correctness. Separate real-image results and geometric measurements would substantially strengthen the reconstruction claims.

The robot experiments establish feasibility but do not isolate the benefit of TabletopGen data. They evaluate three tasks in the original reconstructed setting without an unfine-tuned policy, alternative simulation-data baseline, or held-out scene evaluation. Consequently, they do not yet demonstrate that scene expansion improves policy generalization or quantify the contribution beyond the pretrained policy and domain randomization.

Reproducibility and scalability remain underdocumented. The paper provides useful prompts and DRO settings, but omits important details such as exact ChatGPT model versions, physical parameter assignment, collision tolerances, policy-training settings, and domain-randomization ranges. No end-to-end runtime, API cost, retry rate, or trajectory-generation yield is reported despite repeated claims of efficient, low-cost scaling. The Hunyuan3D-3.0 implementation also cites a 2.5 reference, requiring clarification.

strengths: The contribution is best assessed as Applied/Systems, although no type is explicitly declared: its main value is integrating generative assets, layout recovery, and simulation into a usable manipulation-data pipeline. Under this interpretation, a wholly new algorithm is unnecessary, and the demonstrated system capabilities support a slight preference for acceptance.

The comparative evidence is substantial. Across 78 scenes, TabletopGen improves visual metrics and reduces scene-level collisions to 7.69%, versus 67.95–98.72% for the main image-based baselines. Supplementary comparisons include SceneGen and FlashSculptor, and report 100% support stability and 92.13% dynamic settling stability. These tests provide stronger evidence of simulation usability than visual examples alone.

Human evaluation corroborates the visual improvements: the supplement reports 126 valid questionnaires, randomized presentation, and an overall preference of 83.13%. The qualitative examples also show recognizable, independent objects and more coherent layouts.

The real-robot experiment is a meaningful feasibility demonstration. Policies fine-tuned on 2,000 synthetic trajectories per task achieve 84%, 80%, and 68% real-world success over 50 trials each, including a stacking task. This connects scene generation to practical downstream use.

The presentation is generally clear, with useful intermediate outputs, optimization settings, prompt templates, and component ablations. Removing TSA increases scene-level collisions from 7.69% to 61.54%, supporting the importance of explicit spatial alignment.
weaknesses: The evaluation supports a narrower generalization claim than the paper makes. Section 8.1 reveals that 74 of the 78 inputs are synthesized images and only four are real photographs. Results are not separated by input source, table geometry, or scene difficulty. Consequently, robustness to realistic clutter, occlusion, and photographic variation remains weakly established.

TSA is central but insufficiently specified and its guarantees are overstated. A generated top view and inferred stacking graph do not inherently enforce mesh nonpenetration or valid support. Section 6.2 says objects are rescaled when commonsense sizes deviate significantly, usually only rescaling the table, but gives neither the threshold nor a complete procedure connecting anchor selection to all scale and translation parameters. Figure 25 also instructs the generator to make the tabletop rectangular, creating an unresolved inconsistency with the claimed handling of nonrectangular tables.

The experiments do not cleanly isolate the proposed alignment contribution from stronger upstream generators. The ablations replace DRO and TSA with direct ChatGPT predictions; they do not compare alignment methods using identical generated assets. Comparisons against a depth-based alignment or simple support-constrained placement baseline, alongside anchor-selection and DRO-loss ablations, would better establish the specific technical advance.

The policy-transfer results establish feasibility, but not the claimed reliability of the data engine across environments. All three tasks use one reconstructed real-world setting, and there is no pretrained-policy control, alternative synthetic-data baseline, or alignment ablation in policy learning. The contribution of TabletopGen relative to policy pretraining and domain randomization is therefore unresolved.

Reproducibility and scalability evidence remain incomplete. Despite useful prompts and DRO settings, the manuscript does not report end-to-end runtime, generation cost, retries or failure rates, precise service versions, detailed collision-check tolerances, or sufficient policy-training and physical-parameter settings. These omissions matter for a system presented as fully automatic, low-cost, and scalable.

The visual metrics do not directly establish metric layout accuracy: best-view matching, and even mean-view comparison against a single reference image, cannot measure true pose or scale recovery. Ground-truth geometric evaluation would strengthen this claim. Likewise, the reported 7.69% scene collision rate and 92.13% settling stability warrant more qualified wording than repeated descriptions of collision-free, executable layouts.

strengths: TabletopGen addresses an important computer-vision problem: converting images or text into instance-separated, physically usable scenes for robotic manipulation. The integration of generative asset completion, rotation alignment, top-view layout inference, and simulation is coherent and practically motivated.

The reported improvements are substantial across complementary evaluations. On 78 scenes, scene-level collisions decrease from 67.95–98.72% for the main image-driven baselines to 7.69%. Supplementary Table 5 strengthens the physical-validity evidence with 100% support stability and 92.13% dynamic settling stability, including comparisons with SceneGen and FlashSculptor.

Visual improvements are supported by perceptual metrics, qualitative examples, and a randomized human study, rather than GPT evaluation alone. The reported 83.13% overall preference and higher ratings across all three human-evaluation criteria provide persuasive evidence of perceptual quality.

The downstream demonstration adds meaningful practical evidence: policies fine-tuned using 2,000 synthetic trajectories per task achieve 84%, 80%, and 68% real-world success over 50 trials each. Component ablations also support the usefulness of the proposed alignment stages, particularly TSA.
weaknesses: Real-image generalization is insufficiently established for the breadth of the claims. Section 8.1 reveals that 74 of the 78 evaluation inputs are synthesized and only four are real photographs, without separate quantitative results. The robot experiments concern three tasks in one original real-world scene. These results support feasibility, but not yet broad robustness to real tabletop observations.

The main methodological contribution needs stronger isolation. DRO combines established differentiable silhouette, contour, and feature losses, while TSA relies heavily on generated views and language-model size estimates. Replacing each stage with direct ChatGPT parameter prediction demonstrates usefulness against a weak alternative, but does not isolate RMA anchor selection, the individual rotation losses, or advantages over geometric alignment using the same assets. Different asset-generation backbones also confound attribution of the baseline gains.

TSA's physical and metric-accuracy claims exceed what its formulation guarantees. A synthesized top view does not inherently preserve object locations or enforce containment and nonintersection, and commonsense object dimensions do not establish true metric scale. Moreover, Section 3.2 describes globally deriving scales from the anchor, whereas the supplement describes selectively rescaling objects whose sizes deviate significantly, without specifying the threshold or complete computation. Direct pose/scale errors and sensitivity to top-view or anchor mistakes are missing.

The policy-transfer study establishes executability but does not establish the contribution of TabletopGen to policy performance. There is no pretrained-policy baseline, alternative scene-generation baseline, or alignment ablation evaluated downstream. Training details, randomization ranges, grasp-generation procedures, and simulation-to-robot calibration are insufficiently specified to reproduce these results.

The scalability and full-automation claims lack runtime, hardware, API-cost, retry-rate, and end-to-end generation-yield measurements. Reproducibility also requires precise model versions, collision-detection/contact conventions, and physical-parameter settings. The supplementary prompts and optimizer settings are useful, but do not resolve these operational gaps.
